title: the Beatles and the mantra
hook: a band with every stage open to it goes to an ashram on the Ganges
tomorrow: say a word over and over and it goes empty. why not a mantra?

segments.voice: Gandhi and King ended with a pilgrim, and a hymn that calls the true devotee the one who feels another's pain. Today, another trip to India, with guitars this time.

Some nights the only thing that quiets a loud head is one song on repeat. A famous band, with every stage in the world open to it, went looking for something quieter than a song. The Beatles traveled to an ashram in Rishikesh, a town on the Ganges at the foot of the Himalaya, to learn meditation from a teacher named Maharishi Mahesh Yogi. No crowds, no amplifiers. And what he handed each of them wasn't anything you could hold. It was a word.
screen: `ONE SONG ON REPEAT.` → `AN ASHRAM ON THE GANGES.` → `HE HANDED THEM A WORD.`

segments.voice: The word is mantra. In English it can mean a slogan, something a coach repeats. On the Hindu path it's a sacred sound, word or verse, repeated with attention. The repeating has its own name, japa. Listen to how it sounds in a room: a murmur under the breath, the soft click of beads as a thumb moves one bead along for each round. That string of beads is a mala, and it lets the hand keep count so the mind doesn't have to. The Maharishi's students describe being given a mantra to repeat silently and easily, eyes closed. That made it portable. A Beatle could carry it home to London. But the practice was old long before any band arrived. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names places he can be found: among things that never move, the Himalaya; among rivers, the Ganges. And among offerings, he says, he is japa, the offering of repetition. Not the grand fire ritual. The quiet word, said again. Put the Beatles' story beside that list, and something lines up: the ashram on the Ganges, under the Himalaya, and a word repeated in silence. In the Gita, all three are places Krishna can be found.
screen: `MANTRA: A SACRED SOUND, REPEATED.` · `JAPA, AND THE CLICK OF A MALA.` · `A WORD THAT FITS IN A POCKET.` · `KRISHNA: AMONG OFFERINGS, I AM JAPA.` · then, large: `THE QUIET WORD, SAID AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Hold out one hand, palm up. Choose a word to say softly, a sacred word if you have one, or a plain one like peace, and say it once each time your thumb touches a fingertip, pointer to little finger and back again. Let the thumb and the word keep the same slow pace, and feel the count happen in the hand.
The Beatles and the mantra: a band in Rishikesh, and an old practice, a sacred word repeated with attention.
screen: `THE BEATLES AND THE MANTRA — today's word`.

segments.voice: For the road, from the Beatles and the mantra: in the Gita, the quiet word said again is an offering. More tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1712 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DOESN'T A MANTRA WEAR OUT?`

howItsDone: Hindus practice japa by repeating a mantra or a name of God, aloud, in a whisper or silently, often counting on a mala of beads at a home shrine or during the day.

fork.setup: a friend's yoga teacher gives a 'mantra of the week': i am enough. is that a mantra in the Hindu sense?
options: not quite: a Hindu mantra is a sacred sound or word, repeated with attention.
yes: any phrase repeated often enough turns into a mantra.
no: a mantra only counts if it's in Sanskrit and said out loud.
fork.reveal: on this path a mantra is sacred: a sound, word or verse repeated with attention, aloud or silently. a slogan is something else.

2026-10-14 v3 rewrite (recipe v3, shape senses): sound and touch carry the idea (the murmur of japa, the click of a mala, counting on the fingertips); the practice is physical (finger-tip japa, said softly). 'At the height of its fame' softened to 'with every stage in the world open to it'. Includes new lesson recipe data (chat, gloss, recall); confirm the chat reply, glosses, scripts and pronunciations with the Keeper.
Gita 10.25 names japa among yajnas and the Himalaya among immovable things; 10.31 names the Ganges (Jahnavi) among rivers. The lesson merges them as 'places Krishna can be found'; confirm.
'Handed each of them a word' and silent, easy repetition describe the Maharishi's method as his students describe it; no dates or counts given on purpose. Confirm.
Counting japa on the fingertips (or finger joints) is a known practice; the lesson keeps it simple (fingertips) and doesn't give a bead count. Confirm the mala description.
